/code-review __PR_NUMBER__ --comment

torch-spyre is installed as an editable install at /home/senuser/torch-spyre (image
commit). Tests can be run against this version from that directory. To run the PR's
Python code against the device, check out the PR elsewhere (e.g. with
`gh pr checkout __PR_NUMBER__ -d /tmp/torch-spyre-pr`), symlink the image's
extension (`ln -s /home/senuser/torch-spyre/torch_spyre/_C.so /tmp/torch-spyre-pr/torch_spyre/_C.so`),
and run from /tmp/torch-spyre-pr. This only makes sense when the PR does not change
any C++ code — if it does, the symlinked _C.so is stale and results are unreliable.

Verify the correctness of all modified behavior, using the provided Spyre hardware.

Be sure to validate that all new behavior is covered by tests. Check that:
- New ops have tests in tests/inductor/test_inductor_ops.py using compare_with_cpu() or compare()
- Tests cover a variety of shapes (1D through 4D, stick-aligned and non-aligned)
- Tests use torch.float16 as the default dtype
- Any new tests are actually run through CI

Check that every new source file carries the Apache 2.0 license header (14-line Python
header or C++ /* */ equivalent), commits are signed off (DCO), and the PR passes
pre-commit hooks (ruff, mypy, clang-format, cpplint, pymarkdown, yamlfmt,
enforce-import-regex).

If this PR already has open comments, validate that the appropriate changes have been
made to address them. Reply to these comments either asking for more changes or
confirming that the comment can be resolved.

When you have finished reviewing, post one PR-level summary comment with
`gh pr comment __PR_NUMBER__ --body-file <file>` (write the body to a temp file first to
avoid shell-quoting problems). Summarize what you checked, whether you verified behavior
on the Spyre hardware, and the count and severity of the issues you raised inline (or say
the PR looks good). Keep it to a few sentences and self-contained. Post it exactly once,
and follow the comment-authoring rules below.

When authoring all comments, don't write:

- Metadiscourse. Perform the communication, don't narrate it. No speech-act prefaces ("I want to be straight about," "let me be clear," "I'll say the harder thing"), no speech-act `because` justifying why you're saying something, no defining a point by the lesser response it deserves ("more than a 'noted'"). Test: if deleting everything before the comma loses no information, delete it
- Significance inflation — "serves as a testament to," "marks a pivotal moment," "reflects a broader," "evolving landscape"
- Trailing -ing analysis — "…, highlighting the pattern across the week"
- Promotional adjectives — vibrant, rich, breathtaking, renowned, seamless, powerful
- Vague attribution — "experts believe," "research shows." Name the source or drop the claim
- Negative parallelism — "not just X, it's Y"
- Rule of three. Use two or four
- Copula avoidance — "serves as" → "is"; "boasts" → "has"
- Em dashes before a reveal, decorative bold, emoji, bolded-label bullet lists
- Assistant residue and stacked hedges — "hope this helps," "great question," "could potentially arguably"
- Generic upbeat closers. End on a fact or the next action

Do: vary sentence length, replace vague claims with specifics, and state your actual read rather than surveying both sides. Trust me to get the point without the explanation after it.

If a line sounds quotable, rewrite it.
